original_note: title_bis "Gatos Tuig Bulok" — Tagalog false friend: "bulok" is ROTTEN in Tagalog but means COLOR/hue in Cebuano (rotten = dunot/madunot). The headline reads "Hundred Years Colour" to a Cebuano-only child; the decay fact survives only in the body ("hingpit nga madunot"). ~35 cards corpus-wide use "bulok" this way, so worth the grep.
fact_en: Some kinds of plastic take hundreds of years to fully break down into tiny pieces!
fact_bis: Ang ubang matang sa plastik moabot og gatusan ka tuig una hingpit nga madunot!

original_note: title_bis "Cotton sa Bulok" for "Natural Fibers Rot". Bulok is Tagalog for rotten; in Cebuano bulok means COLOR (cf. ffct-15354 body "walay kolor"), so the headline reads "Cotton in colour" — a different topic. Cebuano for rot is dunot, which the body uses (madunot sa yuta). Title-only, but it is the headline the child sees.
fact_en: Natural fibers like cotton, wool, and silk can rot away in soil since they come from living things — unlike plastic fibers!
fact_bis: Ang natural nga mga hibla sama sa cotton, wool, ug silk madunot sa yuta kay naggikan kini sa buhi nga mga butang — dili sama sa plastik nga hibla!

original_note: title_bis "Bakal Pinakagamit" for 'Iron the Most Used'. 'Bakal' is the Tagalog word for iron; in Bisayan it is the verb to BUY, and Cebuano for iron is 'puthaw' — which is exactly what the card's own body uses, so the title is the outlier. Headline reads as 'buy most-used' rather than naming the metal.
fact_en:
What is the most widely used metal in the world?

Iron is the most used metal for buildings, bridges, and vehicles, but it rusts easily!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang labing kasagarang gamiton nga metal sa kalibotan?

Ang puthaw ang labing kasagarang gamiton sa mga building, taytayan, ug sakyanan, apan dali kining kalawangon!

original_note: title_bis "Pag-uri Basura Bulok Dili" uses Tagalog bulok (rotten). In Cebuano bulok = COLOUR ("unsay bulok sa imong sinina"), so the headline reads "sorting trash by colour or not" — a coherent but wrong sorting criterion for a card about biodegradable vs non-biodegradable. Classic Tagalog false friend; Cebuano rotten = madunot/dunot (the body does say madunot, but the headline states a different, plausible-sounding rule).
fact_en: Sorting trash means separating biodegradable (can rot) from non-biodegradable (cannot rot) kinds! Trash is easier to dispose of or reuse when sorted correctly.
fact_bis: Ang pag-uri sa basura mao ang paglain sa madunot (biodegradable) gikan sa dili madunot (non-biodegradable)! Mas sayon ilabay o magamit pag-usab ang basura kon husto ang pag-uri.

original_note: title_bis "Molubog ang Pako" — in Cebuano pako = WING (also the edible fern), not nail; nail is lansang, which the body itself uses ("lansang nga puthaw"). Tagalog false friend of the langgam class, and it is the headline: the child's headline reads "the wing gets murky/sinks". Verb is off too (lubog = turbid in Cebuano; sink = lunod/unlod, again used correctly in the body). Title was clearly built from the Tagalog term list (terms contain bakal, pako, lumulubog).
fact_en:
Why does a solid iron nail sink?

It sinks because it is heavier than an equal amount of water!
fact_bis:
Nganong maunlod ang solido nga lansang nga puthaw?

Maunlod kini kay mas bug-at kini kaysa sa parehong gidaghanon sa tubig!

original_note: title_bis "Lana Detergent Gamot Pintura" (en "Oil Non-Fuel Products"). In Cebuano gamot = ROOT (medicine = tambal), so the headline reads "Oil Detergent Root Paint" and asserts roots are a product made from oil. The body correctly lists "tambal" but never mentions roots, so nothing in the card explicitly corrects the title word - the child must infer the mapping from a parallel 5-item list. Confirmed Tagalog-false-friend class, in the headline.
fact_en: Oil is also used to make plastics, detergents, medicines, paints, and synthetic cloth—things we use every day!
fact_bis: Gikan sa lana mahimo usab ang plastik, sabon, tambal, pintura, ug sintetikong panapton—mga butang nga gigamit nato adlaw-adlaw!

original_note: title_bis 'Lana sa Karnero' = 'sheep OIL' to a Cebuano reader: lana is oil (esp. coconut oil) in Cebuano, while wool=lana is the Tagalog/Spanish sense. This same batch uses lana for oil three times (ffct-17724 plastik hinimo sa lana, ffct-17729 Polusyon sa Lana, ffct-17757 Molutaw ang Lana), so the corpus' own idiom makes the headline name a different substance than 'Wool from Sheep'. The body never gives a Cebuano word for wool - it keeps the English 'wool' and only describes balahibo sa karnero - so the headline a child sees is left standing as sheep oil.
fact_en:
How does wool from sheep keep us so warm?

Wool comes from thick sheep hair sheared in warm weather! It keeps us warm because tiny air pockets get trapped inside its curly fibers.
fact_bis:
Unsaon pagpabilin nga init nato ang wool gikan sa karnero?

Ang wool naggikan sa baga nga balahibo sa karnero nga guntingon panahon sa init! Init kini kay naay gagmay nga air pockets nga natanggong sa kulot nga fibers.

original_note: title_bis "78 Alak Una Kulob" for "Alcohol Boils Before Water". Cebuano *kulob* = face-down / overturned (Tagalog sense is 'covered/stuffy'); to boil is *bukal*, which the body itself uses ("mobukal una kaysa tubig"). The headline states no boiling at all — it reads "78 alcohol first face-down". Corpus evidence that this is a generator artifact: *kulob* appears in 29 Cebuano TITLES (almost all glossing 'boil') and in 0 bodies, where *bukal* is used throughout; it is even reused for 'wrinkle' in ffct-02691/ffct-05180.
fact_en: Alcohol (ethanol) boils before water! Its boiling point is only about 78°C, while water is 100°C.
fact_bis: Ang alkohol (ethanol) mobukal una kaysa tubig! Ang boiling point niini mga 78°C lang, samtang ang tubig 100°C.

original_note: title_bis "373 Kelvin Kulob" for "Boiling Point 373 Kelvin". The whole point of the card is that 373 K is the BOILING point, and the headline's only content word, *kulob*, means face-down/overturned in Cebuano, not boiling (*bukal*, as the body correctly says). A child reading the headline gets a temperature attached to no process; sibling cards ffct-18572 and ffct-18833 carry the identical bad title.
fact_en: In the Kelvin scale, water boils at about 373 Kelvin (373 K)!
fact_bis: Sa sukat nga Kelvin, ang tubig mobukal sa mga 373 Kelvin (373 K)!

original_note: title_bis "Asin Kulob Taas" for "Salt Raises Boiling Point". *Kulob* is not 'boil' in Cebuano (face-down/overturned); *bukal* is, as the body uses. The headline reduces to "salt face-down high" — the relationship the card teaches (salt raises the boiling point) is not stated in the title at all.
fact_en:
What happens when you add salt to water?

Adding salt to water slightly raises its boiling point above 100°C. It needs a little more heat to start bubbling!
fact_bis:
Unsay mahitabo kung magdugang ka og asin sa tubig?

Ang pagdugang og asin sa tubig gamay nga magpataas sa boiling point niini labaw sa 100°C. Kinahanglan niya og gamay nga kainit aron mobukal!

original_note: title_bis "Bundok Mubu Kulob" for "Boils Below 100 Mountain". Same wrong word: *kulob* (face-down/overturned) standing in for *bukal* (boil), which the body uses correctly ("mobukal ang tubig ubos sa 100°C"). The headline reads "mountain low face-down" and names neither water nor boiling.
fact_en: On a high mountain, water boils below 100°C! This happens because the air pressure there is lower.
fact_bis: Sa habog nga bukid, mobukal ang tubig ubos sa 100°C! Mas huyang kay ang presyon sa hangin didto.
